findings.title: order() is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: order() was added as a new abstract method on the public CryptoProvider SPI. Existing compiled implementations that are not in this PR (custom or older provider jars) no longer satisfy the interface. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider instantiates every provider via ServiceLoader and immediately calls order() to sort, so those implementations fail at startup with AbstractMethodError instead of being ignored. A default method (for example returning 0) would keep old providers loadable and still let the new authz provider lose to explicitly higher-order ones.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider, not BC
findings.body: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the platform keystore provider (typically SunJSSE), not BouncyCastle and not null. Elytron's provider returns null so callers skip BC-specific setup. Callers that do Signature/Cipher.getInstance(alg, provider) with this result look up algorithms only in that provider, which does not implement SHA256withECDSA or the BC padding names Keycloak uses, so ECDSA/JWE operations fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException even though the JDK can perform them. If BouncyIntegration records this provider's name as the crypto provider, later lookups are pinned to the wrong provider for the life of the process.

findings.title: FIPS, Elytron, and default providers share the same order
findings.body: FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and DefaultCryptoProvider all return order 200, while detectProvider now keeps the first provider after a stable sort instead of failing when more than one CryptoProvider is on the classpath. Equal order preserves ServiceLoader/classpath order, so a deployment that contains both the FIPS provider and the default (or Elytron) provider silently runs whichever jar appears first. That can disable FIPS mode without an error. FIPS needs a strictly higher order than the non-FIPS providers now that multiple providers are allowed.

findings.title: ECDSA integer conversion silently truncates oversized components
findings.body: integerToBytes, used by asn1derToConcatenatedRS, copies the low qLength bytes whenever BigInteger.toByteArray() is longer than the curve field size and never checks that the discarded prefix is a single 0x00 sign byte. A non-canonical or oversized ASN.1 INTEGER is therefore rewritten into a different in-range R or S instead of being rejected. Signature conversion then succeeds with a value that is not the one that was signed, so verification can fail closed only by chance, or accept a rewritten component, instead of raising IOException on malformed DER.

findings.title: ECDSA tests use one P-256 key and never check JDK verification
findings.body: The suite generates a single KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") key, which is P-256, and uses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. It only asserts that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip through this provider's own decoder. It never calls Signature.verify on the DER produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER, and ES384/ES512 never see 48-byte or 66-byte R/S values from a matching curve. A DER encoding that Java's strict verifier rejects, or a high-bit padding bug that only shows up at the real ES384/ES512 sizes, still passes.
